title: I Will Love Them Freely
sections: The Lord always invites me to return to Him
Devotion to God must be felt inwardly, not just expressed outwardly
“I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh.”

sayings.text: Ephraim is joined to idols: let him alone.
sayings.speaker: The Lord, about Ephraim
sayings.why: Ephraim, the northern kingdom of Israel, had chosen idols over the Lord. For a time He would leave them to the choice they had made.

sayings.text: Come, and let us return unto the LORD: for he hath torn, and he will heal us
sayings.speaker: Hosea, calling Israel home
sayings.why: Hosea calls the people back: “he hath smitten, and he will bind us up.” The Lord who corrects them is the same One who heals them.

sayings.text: Yet I am become rich, I have found me out substance
sayings.speaker: Ephraim, proud of his riches
sayings.why: Ephraim got rich with “the balances of deceit” (verse 7), cheating people, and then claimed he had done nothing wrong.

sayings.text: O Israel, thou hast destroyed thyself; but in me is thine help.
sayings.speaker: The Lord, to Israel
sayings.why: Israel’s troubles came from its own choices. Even so, the Lord didn’t walk away. Help was still in Him.

sayings.speaker: Israel, back with the Lord
sayings.why: In the last days the Lord will say to Israel, “Thou art my people,” and they will answer Him with these words. The covenant is whole again.

sayings.text: What have I to do any more with idols?
sayings.speaker: Ephraim, turning back to God
sayings.why: Hosea’s book ends with Ephraim repenting: “Ephraim shall say” this, finished with idols for good.

sayings.text: Tell ye your children of it, and let your children tell their children, and their children another generation.
sayings.speaker: Joel, about the locusts
sayings.why: The locusts that stripped the land were so terrible that Joel wanted the lesson remembered for generations.

sayings.text: Spare thy people, O LORD, and give not thine heritage to reproach
sayings.speaker: The priests, weeping at the altar
sayings.why: Joel told the priests to “weep between the porch and the altar” and plead with the Lord for His people.

words.clue: I will ____ thee unto me for ever
words.mean: The Lord promises His people a covenant that will never end, like a faithful marriage.

words.clue: For I desired ____, and not sacrifice
words.mean: The Lord cares more about a loving, faithful heart than about outward offerings.

words.clue: I drew them with ____ of a man, with bands of love
words.mean: The Lord leads His people with love, the way a parent gently guides a child.

words.clue: I will ____ them from the power of the grave
words.mean: Jesus Christ frees us from death. Because of Him, everyone will live again.
When people come back to the Lord, He helps them grow and bloom, like a flower watered by dew.

words.clue: rend your ____, and not your garments
words.mean: God wants us to be truly sorry inside, not just to look sorry on the outside.

words.clue: I will pour out my ____ upon all flesh
words.mean: In our day the Lord pours out His Spirit on everyone who will receive it, young and old.

deep.intro: The lesson asks what these verses teach about the Lord’s love and mercy. Israel has left Him, yet He speaks of winning her back.
deep.q: In Hosea 2:15, what does the Lord say He will make the valley of Achor?
deep.why: Verse 15: “the valley of Achor for a door of hope.” Even after Israel left Him, the Lord opens a way back.
deep.find: the valley of Achor for a door of hope
deep.hunt: In Hosea 2, what does the Lord say He will make the valley of Achor?

deep.intro: The lesson invites you to see how the Savior used Hosea 6:6. Here some Pharisees complain that Jesus eats with publicans and sinners.
deep.q: In Matthew 9:12, who does Jesus say needs a physician?
deep.why: Verse 12: “They that be whole need not a physician, but they that are sick.” Like a doctor who comes for the sick, Jesus came for sinners.
deep.find: They that be whole need not a physician, but they that are sick
deep.hunt: In Matthew 9, who does Jesus say needs a physician?

deep.intro: On the day of Pentecost the Holy Ghost filled Jesus’s disciples, and a crowd gathered. Peter stood up and quoted Joel 2.
deep.q: In Acts 2:15, some people mocked that the disciples were drunk. What does Peter point out?
deep.right: It was only the third hour of the day
wrong: They had fasted for three days
They had been praying in the temple
deep.why: Verse 15: “these are not drunken, as ye suppose, seeing it is but the third hour of the day.” That’s about nine in the morning.
deep.find: seeing it is but the third hour of the day
deep.hunt: In Acts 2, some people mocked that the disciples were drunk. What does Peter point out?

deep.title: From the children’s part of the lesson
deep.intro: The children’s part of this week’s lesson has an idea for Joel 2:28–29 that you can try at the kitchen table.
deep.q: To show what it means for the Spirit to be poured out, the lesson suggests pouring a liquid and comparing it with what?
deep.why: It suggests letting children pour a liquid and then contrasting it with a drip or a trickle. The Lord promised to pour out His Spirit, not just let a little through.
deep.find: contrasting it with a drip or a trickle

deep.title: From For the Strength of Youth
deep.intro: The lesson asks what you can do if you feel the Spirit isn’t being poured out on you. This article answers with seven teachings from the scriptures and apostles.
deep.q: What is the first of the article’s seven ways to increase the flow of revelation?
deep.right: Quiet your environment and your mind
wrong: Write your questions in a journal
Ask your parents for a blessing
deep.why: Number one is to quiet your surroundings and your mind: find a quiet, holy place, then be still before God.
deep.find: Quiet Your Environment and Your Mind

reels.hook: She ran after others. Then she wanted to come home.
reels.body: Hosea’s wife, Gomer, broke her marriage promises and left him. The Lord used this sad story as a picture: Hosea stood for the Lord, and Gomer for Israel, who had left Him to worship false gods. In chapter 2, Israel chases her “lovers” but can’t catch them. At last she says, “I will go and return to my first husband.” Life with the Lord was better all along.

verse.text: And she shall follow after her lovers, but she shall not overtake them; and she shall seek them, but shall not find them: then shall she say, I will go and return to my first husband; for then was it better with me than now.

question.q: Why did Israel decide to go back to her first husband, the Lord?
question.right: Life was better with Him than without
wrong: Her new lovers sent her back home
A prophet ordered her to go back
question.why: “For then was it better with me than now.” The false gods gave her nothing. Coming back to the Lord was coming home.

bonus.q: What does the name Hosea mean, say this week’s Scripture Helps?
wrong: Gift of God, or God gives
bonus.why: They say Hosea’s name means salvation, or Jehovah saves. His whole book is about the Lord saving people who wandered away.

image.alt: Painting of the prophet Hosea in a white robe and red headcloth, raising one hand as he speaks, with a white town behind him
image.credit: Hosea, by James Tissot, about 1900. Public domain

reels.hook: No more calling Him by an idol’s name.
reels.body: Baal was a false god many Israelites worshipped. In Hebrew, Ishi and Baali can both mean my husband, but Baali sounds like the name Baal. So the Lord promised a day when Israel would call Him Ishi, never Baali. He didn’t want His name mixed up with an idol’s. He wants a faithful, loving covenant with His people, like a true marriage.

verse.text: And it shall be at that day, saith the LORD, that thou shalt call me Ishi; and shalt call me no more Baali.

question.q: Why did the Lord want Israel to stop calling Him Baali?
question.right: It sounded like the false god Baal
wrong: It was a name for a foreign king
It was too hard for children to say
question.why: Baali echoes the name Baal. Calling Him Ishi would show Israel had left false gods behind and was faithful to Him.

bonus.q: In Hosea 2:17, what will the Lord take out of Israel’s mouth?
bonus.hunt: In Hosea 2, what will the Lord take out of Israel’s mouth?
bonus.right: The names of the false gods
bonus.why: Verse 17: “I will take away the names of Baalim out of her mouth.” Israel won’t even remember the false gods’ names.
bonus.find: I will take away the names of Baalim out of her mouth

image.alt: A small ancient metal idol of Baal with one arm raised, found at Ugarit in Syria
image.credit: Figure of Baal from Ugarit, 1300s–1100s BC, Louvre. Photo: Jastrow, public domain

reels.hook: He didn’t drag them. He pulled them close with love.
reels.body: The Lord remembers when Israel was young: “I taught Ephraim also to go, taking them by their arms” (Hosea 11:3), like a parent helping a toddler take first steps. He led them with “bands of love,” not chains. He lifted the heavy yoke so they could eat. Even when they turned away, He asked, “How shall I give thee up, Ephraim?” (Hosea 11:8).

verse.text: I drew them with cords of a man, with bands of love: and I was to them as they that take off the yoke on their jaws, and I laid meat unto them.

question.q: In Hosea 11:4, what did the Lord use to lead Israel?
question.why: “I drew them with cords of a man, with bands of love.” The Lord leads by love, not by force.

bonus.q: In Hosea 11:9, why won’t the Lord destroy Ephraim in His anger?
bonus.hunt: In Hosea 11, why won’t the Lord destroy Ephraim in His anger?
bonus.right: He is God, and not a man
bonus.why: Verse 9: “I will not return to destroy Ephraim: for I am God, and not man.” His mercy is bigger than any person’s.
bonus.find: for I am God, and not man

image.alt: Painting of a mother holding up her toddler by the arms as the father kneels in the garden with open arms, waiting for the child’s first steps
image.credit: First Steps, after Millet, by Vincent van Gogh, 1890. Public domain

reels.hook: Even death has to give way to Him.
reels.seek: He promises to rescue His people from dying forever
reels.body: The Lord says, “there is no saviour beside me” (Hosea 13:4). Then He promises something only a Savior can do: “I will redeem them from death.” Redeem means to buy back or set free. Because Jesus Christ died and rose again, everyone will be resurrected. Paul later echoed this verse’s challenge to death: “O death, where is thy sting?” (1 Corinthians 15:55).

verse.text: I will ransom them from the power of the grave; I will redeem them from death: O death, I will be thy plagues; O grave, I will be thy destruction…

question.q: What does the Lord promise in Hosea 13:14?
question.right: To redeem His people from death
wrong: To keep everyone from getting sick
To build a wall around the grave
question.why: “I will ransom them from the power of the grave; I will redeem them from death.” Through Jesus Christ, everyone will live again.

bonus.q: The Friend’s Come, Follow Me page for this week pairs Hosea’s promise about the grave with a Primary song. Which one?
wrong: Can a Little Child Like Me?
Jesus Once Was a Little Child
bonus.why: The Friend says Hosea taught that Jesus Christ would die and be resurrected, so we can live again, and suggests singing Did Jesus Really Live Again?

image.alt: Painting of the resurrected Jesus Christ speaking with Mary Magdalene outside the empty tomb
image.credit: Christ at the Tomb, by Dale Kilbourn

reels.hook: No matter how far you wandered, He still loves you.
reels.body: Hosea ends with an invitation: “O Israel, return unto the LORD thy God” (Hosea 14:1). The Lord promises to heal their backsliding, which means sliding back into old sins. And He will “love them freely,” as a gift He chooses to give. Then He describes people who come back: they grow and bloom like plants watered by morning dew (Hosea 14:5).

verse.text: I will heal their backsliding, I will love them freely: for mine anger is turned away from him.

question.q: What does the Lord promise people who return to Him in Hosea 14:4?
question.right: He will heal them and love them freely
wrong: He will test them for many more years
He will let them come back only once
question.why: “I will heal their backsliding, I will love them freely.” His love isn’t something we have to earn back.

bonus.q: In Hosea 14:9, the last verse of the book, what does Hosea say about the ways of the Lord?
bonus.hunt: In Hosea 14, the last verse of the book, what does Hosea say about the ways of the Lord?
bonus.right: They are right, and the just walk in them
wrong: They are hidden, so no one finds them
They are hard, so few will try them
bonus.why: Verse 9: “for the ways of the LORD are right, and the just shall walk in them.” Coming back means walking His way.
bonus.find: the ways of the LORD are right

image.alt: Yellow and purple wildflowers blooming across a dry, sandy desert wash
image.credit: Wildflowers in a desert wash, Joshua Tree National Park. Photo: NPS / Carmen Aurrecoechea, public domain

reels.hook: Here at sunrise, gone by breakfast.
reels.body: Early in the morning, a cloud or dew can cover the ground. By the time the sun is up, it’s gone. The Lord said Israel’s goodness was like that: it showed up for a moment, then vanished. They still offered sacrifices, but their hearts weren’t really His. The lesson asks what our righteousness should be like. Isaiah’s answer: “as the waves of the sea” (Isaiah 48:18). It keeps coming.

verse.text: O Ephraim, what shall I do unto thee? O Judah, what shall I do unto thee? for your goodness is as a morning cloud, and as the early dew it goeth away.

question.q: Why did the Lord compare Israel’s goodness to the early dew?
question.right: It disappeared as fast as it came
wrong: It made the fields grow very green
It only came on the Sabbath day
question.why: “As the early dew it goeth away.” Their goodness didn’t last. The Lord wants faithfulness that stays.

bonus.q: Hosea 6 mentions the latter and former rain. What did the first rains do for a farmer, says the Old Testament Student Manual?
wrong: Washed the dust off the grapes
Filled the wells for the summer
bonus.why: The manual says the first rains softened the earth so the farmer could plow and plant, and the later rains made the crop grow.
bonus.find: softened the earth so that he could plow it and plant the seed

image.alt: Morning fog lying low across a valley, below sunlit golden hills dotted with pine trees
image.credit: Foggy morning near Tower Junction, Yellowstone National Park. Photo: NPS / Jacob W. Frank, public domain

reels.hook: Jesus quoted this verse to people who judged others.
reels.body: The people of Israel kept offering animal sacrifices, but they had broken their covenant with the Lord (Hosea 6:7). He said He wanted mercy more. Centuries later, some Pharisees complained that Jesus ate with sinners. He told them, “go ye and learn what that meaneth, I will have mercy, and not sacrifice” (Matthew 9:13). Going to church matters. So does how we treat people.

verse.text: For I desired mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.

question.q: What did the Lord want more than burnt offerings?
question.why: “I desired mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.” Offerings mean little without a loving heart.

bonus.q: How many times did Jesus quote this line from Hosea during His ministry, say this week’s Scripture Helps?
bonus.why: They say He quoted it twice, both times correcting Pharisees who cared more about religious rules than about repenting and loving others.
bonus.find: Twice during His mortal ministry, Jesus Christ quoted this statement from the book of Hosea

image.alt: Engraving of Jesus Christ sitting at a low table, sharing a meal with a group of men while a servant brings a dish
image.credit: Jesus Eats with Sinners and Tax Collectors, by Alexandre Bida, 1875. Public domain

reels.hook: Plant good seeds now. You’ll harvest them later.
reels.body: Before planting, farmers break up hard ground that has sat unused. The Lord told Israel to do that with their hearts: “break up your fallow ground.” Plant righteousness, and you’ll harvest mercy. The children’s part of this week’s lesson suggests drawing a clock and writing ways to seek the Lord at different times of day. Morning, school, dinner, bedtime: it’s always a good time to seek Him.

verse.text: Sow to yourselves in righteousness, reap in mercy; break up your fallow ground: for it is time to seek the LORD, till he come and rain righteousness upon you.

question.q: What does Hosea 10:12 say it is time to do?
question.why: “For it is time to seek the LORD, till he come and rain righteousness upon you.” Seeking Him is like planting: the harvest comes.

bonus.q: Which song does this week’s lesson suggest, to teach that it’s always a good time to seek the Lord?
bonus.why: It suggests Anytime, Anywhere, from Hymns for Home and Church. You can seek Him at any hour, wherever you are.

image.alt: A young boy with his arms folded and his eyes closed, praying
image.credit: Prayer, from the Church Media Library

reels.hook: Torn clothes are easy. A changed heart is harder.
reels.body: In Joel’s day, people tore their clothes to show they were sad or sorry. Anyone could rip a robe on the outside. Joel asked for something deeper: “rend your heart, and not your garments.” Rend means tear. The Lord wanted real sorrow and real change inside. And He promised a warm welcome, because He is “gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness.”

verse.text: And rend your heart, and not your garments, and turn unto the LORD your God: for he is gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness, and repenteth him of the evil.

question.q: Why did Joel say to rend your heart instead of your garments?
wrong: New clothes cost too much money
Tearing robes was against the law
question.why: Torn clothes only show on the outside. “Rend your heart” means being truly sorry and turning to the Lord.

bonus.q: In Joel 2:12, besides all your heart, what three things does the Lord say to turn to Him with?
bonus.hunt: In Joel 2, besides all your heart, what three things does the Lord say to turn to Him with?
bonus.why: Verse 12: “turn ye even to me with all your heart, and with fasting, and with weeping, and with mourning.” They showed they meant it.
bonus.find: with fasting, and with weeping, and with mourning

image.alt: Painting of the prophet Joel in a long dark robe, standing in a garden with both hands pressed over his heart
image.credit: Joel, by Charles Hoffbauer after James Tissot, 1904. Photo: Phillip Medhurst, CC BY-SA 4.0

reels.hook: Kids, grandparents, everyone: God’s Spirit for all.
reels.body: Joel saw a day when the Lord would “pour out my spirit upon all flesh.” Not just on prophets: “your sons and your daughters shall prophesy.” Old men would dream dreams, and young men see visions. When the angel Moroni first visited young Joseph Smith, he quoted these verses and said they would soon come true (Joseph Smith—History 1:41). That’s our day. The Holy Ghost can guide you too.

verse.text: And it shall come to pass afterward, that I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh; and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, your old men shall dream dreams, your young men shall see visions:

question.q: In Joel 2:28, who will receive the Lord’s Spirit?
question.why: “I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh.” Sons, daughters, old men and young men: that includes you.

bonus.q: In Joel 2:29, who else will the Lord pour His Spirit upon?
bonus.hunt: In Joel 2, besides sons, daughters, old men and young men, who else will the Lord pour His Spirit upon?
bonus.why: Verse 29: “And also upon the servants and upon the handmaids in those days will I pour out my spirit.” No one is left out.
bonus.find: upon the servants and upon the handmaids

image.alt: Painting of the angel Moroni in a white robe standing in the air beside young Joseph Smith, who sits up in bed in his log-cabin room
image.credit: Moroni Appears to Joseph Smith in His Room, by Tom Lovell

reels.hook: What the bugs ate, God promises to give back.
reels.body: Joel’s people had watched swarms of locusts, a kind of grasshopper, strip their fields bare (Joel 1:4). Some years there was nothing left to harvest. But the Lord made a promise: “I will restore to you the years that the locust hath eaten.” Rain would come again, and the floors would be “full of wheat” (verse 24). The Lord can make up for what we lose, too.

verse.text: And I will restore to you the years that the locust hath eaten, the cankerworm, and the caterpiller, and the palmerworm, my great army which I sent among you.

question.q: What does the Lord promise in Joel 2:25?
question.right: To give back the years the locusts ate
wrong: To send even more locusts next year
To move His people to a new land
question.why: “I will restore to you the years that the locust hath eaten.” He can heal and replace what was lost.

bonus.q: In Joel 1, the palmerworm is the Hebrew word gazam. What does it mean, says the Old Testament Student Manual?
bonus.why: The manual says gazam means gnawer. Joel’s four names for the insects describe stages of a locust’s life, each eating what the last one left.
bonus.find: The palmerworm is the Hebrew gazam, which means “gnawer.”

image.alt: Pink fireweed flowers and green plants growing up through black ash among burned trees after a forest fire
image.credit: Fireweed grows in a burned area, Kenai National Wildlife Refuge, Alaska. Photo: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, public domain

reels.hook: Crowds and crowds, and a choice to make.
reels.body: Joel saw huge crowds of nations gathering before the Second Coming, in a place he called “the valley of decision.” The battle won’t go their way: the Lord is stronger than every army. In a way, each of us stands in a valley of decision now: will we choose the Lord? Joel ends with a promise for those who do: “the LORD dwelleth in Zion” (Joel 3:21).

verse.text: Multitudes, multitudes in the valley of decision: for the day of the LORD is near in the valley of decision.

question.q: What did Joel call the place where the multitudes gather?
question.why: “Multitudes, multitudes in the valley of decision.” The day of the Lord is coming, and everyone must choose.

bonus.q: In Joel 3:16, when the heavens and the earth shake, what will the Lord be to His people?
bonus.hunt: In Joel 3, when the heavens and the earth shake, what will the Lord be to His people?
bonus.why: Verse 16: “the LORD will be the hope of his people, and the strength of the children of Israel.” His people don’t need to fear.
bonus.find: the LORD will be the hope of his people

image.alt: Painting of a deep, rocky valley below the walls of Jerusalem, with a village on the far hillside and sheep grazing in front
image.credit: Jerusalem and the Valley of Jehoshaphat from the Hill of Evil Counsel, by Thomas Seddon, about 1854. Public domain

lines: The Lord tells Hosea to marry. Hosea marries Gomer, and his family becomes a sign to Israel, which has been unfaithful to the Lord. (verses 1–3)
Their three children get names that warn Israel: Jezreel, Lo-ruhamah (no more mercy), and Lo-ammi (not my people). (verses 4–9)
Yet in the day of gathering, Israel will be as many as the sand of the sea and be called sons of the living God. (verses 10–11)

review.about: The KJV’s “wife of whoredoms” is told gently, as the lesson does: Gomer’s unfaithfulness is a sign of Israel’s, and line 1 says no more than that.
“No more mercy” follows the verse’s own words for Lo-ruhamah; the Scripture Helps give “not pitied” or “not having obtained mercy.”

lines: Israel is like a wife who left her husband for other lovers: false gods she thinks gave her food and clothes. (verses 1–5)
When she can’t find them, she wants to go back. The Lord, who gave her everything, will take it away because she served Baal. (verses 6–13)
Then He will win her back and speak tenderly to her, and she will call Him Ishi, my husband. (verses 14–17)
In the last days He will bring peace and marry Israel forever. They will be His people, and He their God. (verses 18–23)

review.about: “Ishi, my husband” follows the Old Testament Student Manual’s gloss; the line leaves out verse 17 (the names of Baalim), a bonus answer.
“Marry Israel forever” is verse 19’s “betroth thee unto me for ever,” and the heading’s “reconciled to God.”

lines: The Lord tells Hosea to love his wife again, as the Lord loves Israel. Hosea pays to bring her back home. (verses 1–3)
Israel will live many days without a king or sacrifices. In the latter days they will return and seek the Lord and His goodness. (verses 4–5)

review.about: The woman in verse 1 is taken to be Gomer, as the lesson and Scripture Helps tell it (Hosea’s efforts to bring her back).

lines: The Lord has a case against Israel: there is no truth, mercy, or knowledge of God. Lying, stealing and killing fill the land. (verses 1–3)
His people are destroyed because they reject knowledge, and the priests are as bad as the people. (verses 4–10)
They ask wooden idols for advice and worship on the hills. Israel is like a stubborn young cow, and Ephraim is joined to idols. (verses 11–19)

review.about: “Wooden idols” for the KJV’s “stocks” follows the Old Testament Student Manual.

lines: Israel’s priests and leaders have trapped the people like a hunter’s net. Their pride shows, and both Israel and Judah will fall. (verses 1–7)
Ephraim and Judah are sick and wounded. Ephraim runs to Assyria for help, but Assyria can’t heal them. (verses 8–14)
The Lord will go away until they admit their sins and seek Him. (verse 15)
Hosea calls Israel to return to the Lord, who will heal them. He will come to them as surely as morning and rain. (verses 1–3)
But their goodness disappears like a morning cloud. The Lord wants mercy and knowing Him more than sacrifices. (verses 4–6)
They have broken the covenant. Even the priests do murder, and Israel is unclean. (verses 7–11)
Israel is an empty vine. The richer they got, the more altars and idols they built, so those will be torn down. (verses 1–8)
Israel has sinned since the days of Gibeah, and the Lord will correct them. (verses 9–11)
Hosea calls them to plant righteousness and seek the Lord. They have plowed wickedness, so their forts will fall. (verses 12–15)
The Lord loved Israel as a child and called him out of Egypt, like Jesus, who came out of Egypt as a child. (verse 1)
He taught Ephraim to walk and led them with love, but they turned to idols, and Assyria will rule them. (verses 2–7)
The Lord can’t give Ephraim up. He will bring His people home, though Ephraim still lies to Him. (verses 8–12)

review.about: The comparison to Jesus comes from the chapter heading (“in similitude of our Lord”) and Matthew 2:15.
The line leaves out verse 9’s reason (“I am God, and not man”), a bonus answer.

lines: Ephraim chases the wind and makes deals with Assyria and Egypt, and the Lord will judge Jacob’s family. (verses 1–2)
Jacob wrestled with the angel and met God at Bethel. So turn to God, keep mercy and justice, and wait on Him. (verses 3–6)
Ephraim cheats to get rich, then says he has done nothing wrong. (verses 7–9)
The Lord guided His people by prophets, visions and similitudes, or symbols, yet Ephraim angered Him bitterly. (verses 10–14)
Ephraim keeps sinning and making idols, so they will vanish like morning mist and smoke. (verses 1–3)
The Lord brought them out of Egypt. There is no Savior but Him, yet they forgot Him. (verses 4–8)
Israel ruined itself, but its help is in the Lord. He will ransom them from the grave and redeem them from death. (verses 9–14)
An east wind will dry up Ephraim, and Samaria will fall for rebelling against God. (verses 15–16)
Hosea pleads with Israel to return to the Lord with words of repentance, instead of trusting Assyria or idols. (verses 1–3)
The Lord will heal them and love them freely. He will be like dew, and Israel will grow like a lily and an olive tree. (verses 4–7)
Ephraim will be done with idols, and Hosea ends by asking who is wise enough to understand. (verses 8–9)

review.about: The heading says this happens “in the last days”; the line keeps to what the verses say, an invitation to return.
Verse 9’s “the ways of the LORD are right” is a bonus answer, so the line only names its question.

lines: Joel tells the people to tell their children about a terrible plague of locusts that ate everything. (verses 1–4)
An invader like a lion has stripped the vines and fig trees, and the offerings at the temple have stopped. (verses 5–12)
The priests must fast, call a solemn assembly, and gather everyone to the house of the Lord, for the day of the Lord is near. (verses 13–15)
The food is gone, the animals groan, and fire has burned the fields. Joel cries to the Lord. (verses 16–20)
Before the Second Coming, a great army will bring war and ruin, and the sun and moon will go dark. (verses 1–11)

review.about: “Whoredoms” and “adulteries” are “unfaithfulness” and “unfaithful ways,” as asked. “From between her breasts” is kept as the KJV has it, no plainer than scripture; “from her heart” or “from her body” would be softer but less exact. Your call. “Plead” (argue a case, as in court) is “argue with.”

“Played the harlot” is “been unfaithful” here; “lewdness” (verse 10) is “shame”; and the KJV’s “rewards” (verse 12), a word for a harlot’s pay, is just “pay.” The “lovers” are the false gods she thanks for her food (verse 8).
The Hebrew and the KJV switch from “thy way” to “she”; the plain words keep the switch (“your road … around her”), where the BSB smooths it to ‘her path.’

Ishi, Baali, Ammi, Ruhamah, Achor and Jezreel get their meanings in a few words (the Church’s footnotes give the first five). Jezreel means ‘God plants’ (verse 22), which is why verse 23 says “I will plant her.”
“Betroth” (promise to marry) is “make you my bride,” to keep it plain. The KJV’s “hear” in verses 21–22 is “answer,” the Hebrew word’s usual meaning (BSB ‘respond’).

verses: Then the Lord said to me, “Go again and love a woman who is loved by another man and is unfaithful, just as the Lord loves the children of Israel, even though they turn to other gods and love raisin cakes (used in worshipping idols).”
So I bought her for myself for fifteen pieces of silver and a homer and a half of barley.
Then I said to her, “You must stay with me for many days. You must not be unfaithful or belong to another man, and I will be yours too.”
For the children of Israel will live for many days without a king or a prince, without sacrifice or sacred pillar, and without an ephod (a priest’s apron) or teraphim (household idols).
Afterward the children of Israel will come back and seek the Lord their God and David their king. They will come trembling to the Lord and to His goodness in the latter days.

notes.text: The KJV says “flagons of wine.” The Hebrew means cakes of raisins, which were used in worshipping false gods; the BSB has ‘love to offer raisin cakes to idols.’

review.about: “An adulteress” is “unfaithful,” as asked. “Beloved of her friend” is “loved by another man” (BSB ‘loved by another’); the Hebrew word means a companion. “(used in worshipping idols)” follows the Church’s footnote on “flagons of wine,” which gives raisin cakes used in false worship.
“Thou shalt not play the harlot” is “You must not be unfaithful.” “So will I also be for thee” is “I will be yours too.”
“An homer … and an half homer” is “a homer and a half”; the Hebrew’s second measure is a lethech (BSB), which the KJV gives as half a homer.

verses: Hear the word of the Lord, you children of Israel, for the Lord has a case against the people who live in the land, because there is no truth, no mercy, and no knowledge of God in the land.
There is swearing, lying, murder, stealing, and adultery. They break all limits, and one killing follows another.
So the land will mourn, and everyone who lives in it will waste away, along with the wild animals and the birds of the sky. Even the fish of the sea will be taken away.
But let no one argue or blame anyone else, for your people are like those who argue with a priest.
So you will fall in the daytime, and the prophet will fall with you at night, and I will destroy your mother.

My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge. Because you have rejected knowledge, I will also reject you from being my priest. Since you have forgotten the law of your God, I will also forget your children.
The more they grew, the more they sinned against me. So I will change their glory into shame.
They feed on the sin of my people and set their hearts on their wickedness.
It will be the same for the people and the priest: I will punish them for their ways and pay them back for what they have done.
They will eat but not have enough. They will be unfaithful but will not grow in number, because they have stopped paying attention to the Lord.
Unfaithfulness, wine, and new wine take away understanding.
My people ask advice from a piece of wood, and their stick gives them answers. For a spirit of unfaithfulness has led them astray, and they have been unfaithful, leaving their God.

They offer sacrifices on the mountaintops and burn incense on the hills, under oaks, poplars, and terebinths, because their shade is pleasant. So your daughters are unfaithful, and your daughters-in-law are unfaithful to their husbands.

I will not punish your daughters when they are unfaithful, or your daughters-in-law when they are unfaithful to their husbands, because the men themselves go off with harlots and offer sacrifices with the women of the idol shrines. A people without understanding will fall.
Though you, Israel, are unfaithful, don’t let Judah become guilty too. Don’t go to Gilgal, don’t go up to Beth-aven (house of wickedness), and don’t swear, “As the Lord lives.”
For Israel is stubborn, like a stubborn young cow. Now the Lord will feed them like a lamb in a wide-open place.
Ephraim is joined to idols. Leave him alone.
Their drink has gone sour. They are unfaithful again and again. Her rulers dearly love shame.
A wind has wrapped her up in its wings, and they will be ashamed because of their sacrifices.

notes.text: The KJV ends, “her rulers with shame do love, Give ye.” The Church’s footnote gives another reading, ‘deeply love dishonor,’ and the BSB has ‘their rulers dearly love disgrace.’

review.about: “Adultery” is kept here, the commandment’s word in a list of crimes, as in Jeremiah 7:9. Elsewhere in Hosea “whoredom” is “unfaithful.” “They break out, and blood toucheth blood” follows the Church’s footnotes (‘break all bounds’; ‘bloodshed leads to bloodshed’).

Verses 13–14 are about real sin at idol shrines. “Commit whoredom” is “are unfaithful,” “commit adultery” is “are unfaithful to their husbands,” “whores” is “harlots” (the KJV’s word, kept in Isaiah 1:21), and the KJV’s “harlots” (women who served at the shrines) are “the women of the idol shrines.” Check these are right for Javan. “Spouses” is “daughters-in-law” (BSB); the Hebrew word means brides.
The plain words keep the KJV’s statement. The BSB reads the second half as a question: ‘Can the LORD now shepherd them like lambs in an open meadow?’ No note.
Hard Hebrew. The plain words follow the Church’s footnote for the last line and leave out the KJV’s “Give ye,” which reads one Hebrew word another way; there is a note.

verses: Hear this, you priests! Pay attention, house of Israel! Listen, house of the king! This judgment is for you, because you have been a trap at Mizpah and a net spread out on Tabor.
The rebels have gone deep into killing, though I have corrected them all.
I know Ephraim, and Israel is not hidden from me. For now, Ephraim, you have been unfaithful, and Israel is unclean.
Their deeds won’t let them turn back to their God, because a spirit of unfaithfulness is inside them, and they do not know the Lord.
Israel’s pride testifies against him. So Israel and Ephraim will fall in their sin, and Judah will fall with them too.
They will go with their flocks and herds to seek the Lord, but they won’t find Him. He has pulled away from them.
They have betrayed the Lord, for they have had children who are strangers to Him. Now, within a month, they and everything they own will be eaten up.
Blow the ram’s horn in Gibeah and the trumpet in Ramah. Sound the alarm at Beth-aven: “Behind you, Benjamin!”
Ephraim will become a ruin on the day of punishment. Among the tribes of Israel I have made known what will surely happen.
The leaders of Judah are like those who move a boundary marker to steal land. I will pour out my anger on them like water.
Ephraim is oppressed and crushed in judgment, because he was determined to follow the command.
So I will be like a moth to Ephraim, and like rot to the house of Judah.
When Ephraim saw his sickness and Judah saw his wound, Ephraim went to the Assyrian and sent to King Jareb. But he cannot heal you or cure your wound.
For I will be like a lion to Ephraim and like a young lion to the house of Judah. I, yes I, will tear them to pieces and go away. I will carry them off, and no one will rescue them.
Then I will go back to my place until they admit their guilt and seek my face. In their trouble they will search hard for me.

notes.text: The KJV says “walked after the commandment.” The Hebrew word is rare. The Church’s footnote gives another reading, ‘after filth,’ and the BSB has ‘follow worthless idols.’
The KJV takes Jareb as a king’s name. The Hebrew can also mean ‘the great king,’ as the BSB has it, here and in Hosea 10:6.

review.about: “They will not frame their doings to turn unto their God” follows the Church’s footnote: ‘Their behavior does not permit them to return.’

“Dealt treacherously” is “betrayed.” “Strange children” is “children who are strangers to Him” (BSB ‘illegitimate children’), the modest way to say it. “Now shall a month devour them with their portions” follows the Church’s footnote: ‘Within a month they and their property shall be destroyed.’
“Remove the bound” (a boundary marker, the Church’s footnote) adds three words, “to steal land,” to say why it was wrong (Deuteronomy 19:14).
Unsure Hebrew; the plain words follow the KJV (“the command”), with a note giving the footnote’s and the BSB’s readings.

verses: Come, let us go back to the Lord. He has torn us to pieces, but He will heal us. He has struck us down, but He will bandage our wounds.
After two days He will bring us back to life. On the third day He will raise us up, and we will live in His presence.
Let us know the Lord—let us keep pressing on to know Him. He will come out as surely as the dawn. He will come to us like the rain, like the spring rain and the winter rain on the earth.
Ephraim, what can I do with you? Judah, what can I do with you? Your goodness is like a morning cloud, like the early dew that goes away.
That is why I have cut them down by the prophets; I have killed them with the words of my mouth. And your judgments go out like the light.
For I want mercy, not sacrifice, and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.
But like men, they have broken the covenant. There they have betrayed me.
Gilead is a city of people who do evil, and it is marked with bloody footprints.
Like gangs of robbers lying in wait for someone, so a band of priests murder on the road to Shechem. They have done shameful, wicked things.
I have seen a horrible thing in the house of Israel: Ephraim’s unfaithfulness is there, and Israel is unclean.
Also, Judah, a harvest has been set for you, when I bring my people back from captivity.

notes.text: Jesus quoted this verse when He ate with sinners, and again when His disciples picked grain on the Sabbath (Matthew 12:7): “I will have mercy, and not sacrifice” (Matthew 9:13).
The KJV says “like men.” The Hebrew word adam means man, and it is also the name Adam; the Church’s footnote gives ‘Adam,’ and the BSB reads ‘like Adam.’
The KJV says “in the way by consent.” The Church’s footnote gives the Hebrew as ‘on the road to Shechem,’ as the BSB has it.

review.about: “Revive us” is “bring us back to life,” as the Church’s footnote has it (‘restore us to life; i.e., resurrect us’). “The latter and former rain” (verse 3) is the spring and winter rain, as the footnote there says.
The KJV reads “Then shall we know, if we follow on to know the LORD”; the Hebrew is “let us know, let us press on to know” (BSB), and the plain words follow the Hebrew.
The KJV and the Hebrew have “thy judgments are as the light”; the BSB reads ‘My judgments go forth like lightning,’ dividing the letters another way. The plain words follow the KJV; no note.

The plain words follow the Hebrew and the Church’s footnote (“on the road to Shechem”) over the KJV’s “by consent,” with a note. “Commit lewdness” is “done shameful, wicked things.” In verse 8, “polluted with blood” is the Hebrew picture, “marked with bloody footprints.”

verses: Israel is an empty vine; he produces fruit for himself. The more fruit he had, the more altars he built. The better his land did, the finer he made his sacred pillars.
Their heart is divided; now they will be found guilty. It is He who will break down their altars and destroy their sacred pillars.
Now they will say, “We have no king, because we did not fear the Lord. And what could a king do for us?”
They speak empty words and swear false oaths when they make a covenant. So judgment springs up like poisonous weeds in the furrows of a field.

The people of Samaria will be afraid for the calf idols of Beth-aven. Its people will mourn over it, and so will its idol priests who rejoiced over it and its glory, because its glory has been carried away from it.
It will also be carried to Assyria as a gift for King Jareb. Ephraim will be put to shame, and Israel will be ashamed of its own plans.
As for Samaria, her king will be cut off like foam on the water.
The high places of Aven, the sin of Israel, will be destroyed. Thorns and thistles will grow up over their altars. And they will say to the mountains, “Cover us!” and to the hills, “Fall on us!”
Israel, you have sinned ever since the days of Gibeah. There they stood. The battle against the wicked in Gibeah did not catch up with them.
When I choose, I will punish them. Nations will gather against them when they are bound for their two sins.
Ephraim is a trained young cow that loves to thresh grain, but I have come to put a yoke on her fine neck. I will harness Ephraim; Judah will plow, and Jacob will break up the clods.
Sow righteousness for yourselves, and reap mercy. Break up your unplowed ground, for it is time to seek the Lord, until He comes and rains righteousness on you.
You have plowed wickedness and harvested sin; you have eaten the fruit of lies, because you trusted in your own way and in your many mighty men.

So the roar of battle will rise among your people, and all your fortresses will be destroyed, the way Shalman destroyed Beth-arbel on the day of battle, when mothers were dashed to pieces with their children.
This is what Beth-el will bring on you, because of your great wickedness. At dawn the king of Israel will be completely cut off.

notes.text: The KJV says “an empty vine.” The Hebrew word usually means emptied, but here the BSB reads it as ‘a luxuriant vine,’ one spreading and full of fruit.
On His way to the cross, Jesus told the women weeping for Him that people would say “to the mountains, Fall on us; and to the hills, Cover us” (Luke 23:30).
The KJV says “in their two furrows.” The Hebrew, as it is read aloud, says ‘their two iniquities,’ and the BSB has ‘for their double transgression.’

review.about: “Goodly images” are the Hebrew’s sacred pillars, standing stones set up for false worship (verse 2 too). “Empty vine” follows the KJV, with a note for the BSB’s ‘luxuriant vine.’
“It is He who” is the Hebrew’s strong “he,” capitalized for God; the BSB makes it ‘The LORD.’ “Found faulty” is “found guilty,” as the Church’s footnote has it (‘HEB guilty’).

Hard Hebrew. The plain words keep the KJV’s statement; the BSB reads the last line as a question, ‘Did not the battle in Gibeah overtake the sons of iniquity?’ Gibeah was where Israel once fought the tribe of Benjamin over a terrible crime (Judges 19–20); no note.
The plain words follow the Hebrew as it is read (“their two sins”) over the KJV’s “two furrows,” with a note.
“I passed over upon her fair neck” means putting a yoke on it (BSB ‘I will place a yoke on her fair neck’); the plain words add “to put a yoke on.” “Make Ephraim to ride” is “harness Ephraim.”
The last line, mothers dashed to pieces with their children, is kept no plainer than the KJV.

verses: When Israel was a child, I loved him, and I called my son out of Egypt.
The more they were called, the farther they went from those who called them. They sacrificed to the Baalim (the false gods called Baal) and burned incense to carved idols.
I was the one who taught Ephraim to walk, taking them by their arms, but they didn’t know that I healed them.
I led them with cords of kindness, with ropes of love. To them I was like someone who lifts the yoke off their jaws, and I bent down and fed them.
He will not go back to the land of Egypt, but the Assyrian will be his king, because they refused to turn back.
The sword will fall on his cities and destroy his branches and eat them up, because of their own plans.
My people are set on turning away from me. Even though they are called to the Most High, not one of them honors Him.

How can I give you up, Ephraim? How can I hand you over, Israel? How can I make you like Admah, or treat you like Zeboim (cities destroyed with Sodom)? My heart is turned inside me; all my compassion is stirred up.
I will not carry out my fierce anger. I will not destroy Ephraim again, for I am God and not a man—the Holy One among you—and I will not enter the city.
They will follow the Lord. He will roar like a lion. When He roars, the children will come trembling from the west.
They will come trembling like birds out of Egypt and like doves out of the land of Assyria, and I will settle them in their homes, says the Lord.
Ephraim surrounds me with lies, and the house of Israel with deceit. But Judah still walks with God and is faithful with the saints.

notes.text: Matthew says this was fulfilled in Jesus, whose family stayed in Egypt until King Herod died: “Out of Egypt have I called my son” (Matthew 2:15).
The Joseph Smith Translation says the Lord’s heart is turned ‘toward thee, and my mercies are extended to gather thee,’ in place of “within me, my repentings are kindled together.”
The KJV says “I will not enter into the city.” The Church’s footnote gives another reading, ‘come in anger,’ and the BSB has ‘I will not come in wrath.’

review.about: “As they called them, so they went from them” is “The more they were called, the farther they went from those who called them.” The BSB reads ‘the more I called Israel.’
“Cords of a man” (ropes for people, not for animals) is “cords of kindness,” as the BSB has it. Check you’re happy with that.

“My repentings” is “my compassion,” what the Hebrew word means (BSB ‘My compassion is stirred’). The note gives the Joseph Smith Translation, from the Church’s footnote. Admah and Zeboim are explained in four words (Deuteronomy 29:23).
“Judah yet ruleth with God” is “walks with God,” the reading in the Church’s footnote (‘OR walks’) and the BSB. “The saints” is kept from the KJV; the BSB reads ‘the Holy One.’ No note.

verses: Ephraim feeds on the wind and chases the east wind. All day long he piles up lies and ruin. They make a covenant with the Assyrians, and olive oil is carried to Egypt.
The Lord also has a case against Judah. He will punish Jacob for his ways and pay him back for what he has done.
In the womb he took his brother by the heel, and by his strength he struggled with God.
Yes, he struggled with the angel and won. He wept and begged him for favor. At Beth-el he found Him, and there He spoke with us—
the Lord God of Hosts; the Lord is the name He is remembered by.
So turn back to your God. Hold on to mercy and justice, and always wait for your God.
He is a merchant with dishonest scales in his hand; he loves to cheat.
Ephraim says, “I have become rich; I have found wealth for myself. In all my work no one will find any wrong in me that is sin.”
But I am the Lord your God from the time you were in the land of Egypt. I will make you live in tents again, as in the days of the appointed feast.
I have spoken through the prophets. I gave many visions and taught with parables through the prophets.
Is there wickedness in Gilead? Surely they are worthless. They sacrifice bulls in Gilgal, and their altars are like piles of stones in the furrows of the fields.
Jacob ran away to the country of Syria. Israel worked to earn a wife, and to pay for a wife he kept sheep.
The Lord brought Israel out of Egypt by a prophet, and by a prophet Israel was kept safe.
Ephraim has made Him bitterly angry. So his Lord will leave his blood guilt on him and pay him back for his contempt.

notes.text: The KJV says “there he spake with us.” The Church’s footnote gives another reading, ‘him,’ and the BSB has ‘spoke with Him there.’

review.about: Verses 3–4 retell Jacob’s life: taking Esau’s heel at birth and wrestling the angel (Genesis 25:26; 32:24–30). The plain words don’t name Esau or add the story; no note.
Lowercase “he” is Jacob; capital “Him” and “He” are God, who spoke at Beth-el (verse 5 names Him). “Made supplication unto him” is “begged him for favor.” Check the capitals read right.
“Tabernacles” is “tents,” as the Church’s footnote has it; the appointed feast is the Feast of Tabernacles (Leviticus 23:34). No note.
“His blood” is “his blood guilt,” as the Church’s footnote has it (‘IE guilt’). “His reproach” is “his contempt.” “His Lord” is capitalized, as in the KJV.

verses: When Ephraim spoke, there was trembling, and he was lifted up in Israel. But he became guilty by worshipping Baal, and he died.

And now they sin more and more. They have made metal idols out of their silver, idols shaped by their own skill, all of it the work of craftsmen. They say of them, “Let the men who sacrifice kiss the calves!”
So they will be like the morning cloud, like the early dew that goes away, like chaff blown by a storm from the threshing floor, and like smoke out of a chimney.
Yet I am the Lord your God from the land of Egypt. You must know no god but me, for there is no Savior besides me.
I knew you in the wilderness, in the land of great drought.
When they had pasture, they were filled. They were filled, and their hearts became proud, so they forgot me.
So I will be like a lion to them; like a leopard I will watch for them by the road.
I will meet them like a bear robbed of her cubs, and I will tear open their chests. There I will eat them up like a lion; the wild animals will tear them apart.
Israel, you have destroyed yourself, but your help is in me.
I will be your king. Where is anyone else who can save you in all your cities? And where are your judges, the ones you asked for when you said, “Give me a king and leaders”?
In my anger I gave you a king, and in my fury I took him away.
Ephraim’s wickedness is tied up in a bundle; his sin is stored away.
Pains like a woman giving birth will come on him. He is an unwise son, for when the time comes, he does not come out of the womb.
I will ransom them from the power of the grave. I will redeem them from death. Death, I will be your plagues! Grave, I will be your destruction! I will not change my mind.

Even though he does well among his brothers, an east wind will come, the wind of the Lord rising up from the wilderness. His spring will dry up, and his fountain will run dry. He will rob his storehouse of every precious thing.

Samaria will bear her guilt, because she has rebelled against her God. They will fall by the sword. Their little children will be dashed to pieces, and their women who are expecting babies will be ripped open.

notes.text: The KJV has “Let the men that sacrifice kiss the calves.” The Hebrew can also be read ‘those who sacrifice people,’ and the BSB has ‘They offer human sacrifice and kiss the calves!’
Speaking of the God who brought Israel out of Egypt, Nephi taught that “there is none other name given under heaven save it be this Jesus Christ … whereby man can be saved” (2 Nephi 25:20).
The KJV reads “I will be thy king.” The Hebrew word can also mean ‘where,’ and the BSB reads ‘Where is your king now to save you in all your cities?’
Paul uses these words about the Resurrection: “O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?” (1 Corinthians 15:55). Where the KJV has “I will be,” the BSB also reads ‘Where.’
The KJV says “Samaria shall become desolate.” The Hebrew word means to be held guilty, and the BSB has ‘Samaria will bear her guilt.’

review.about: The KJV reads “When Ephraim spake trembling, he exalted himself”; the BSB, ‘When Ephraim spoke, there was trembling; he was exalted.’ The plain words follow the Hebrew’s order, like the BSB. No note.

The plain words keep the KJV, “in me is thine help.” The BSB reads the hard Hebrew another way: ‘You are destroyed, O Israel, because you are against Me—against your helper.’ No note; add one if you like.

The KJV’s promise is kept (“I will be your plagues”), with a note for Paul’s and the BSB’s ‘where.’ “Repentance shall be hid from mine eyes” is “I will not change my mind”; the Church’s footnote gives ‘compassion’ for the Hebrew word, and the BSB reads ‘Compassion is hidden from My eyes,’ a warning. Your call.
The last line, children and women killed in war, is kept no plainer than the KJV. “Become desolate” follows the Hebrew (“bear her guilt”), with a note.
“The caul of their heart” (the Church’s footnote: ‘chamber’) is “their chests.” Kept no plainer than the KJV.

verses: Israel, come back to the Lord your God, for you have fallen because of your sin.
Take words with you and come back to the Lord. Say to Him, “Take away all sin, and receive us kindly, and we will offer our lips as calves for sacrifice.”
Asshur (Assyria) will not save us. We will not ride on horses. We will never again say to the things our hands have made, “You are our gods,” for in you the fatherless find mercy.
I will heal them of turning away. I will love them freely, for my anger has turned away from him.
I will be like the dew to Israel. He will bloom like the lily and send down his roots like the cedars of Lebanon.
His branches will spread out. His beauty will be like the olive tree, and his fragrance like the cedars of Lebanon.
Those who live in his shade will come back. They will come back to life like grain and blossom like the vine. His fragrance will be like the wine of Lebanon.
Ephraim will say, “What more do I have to do with idols?” I have answered him, and I will watch over him. I am like a green fir tree; your fruit comes from me.
Who is wise? Let him understand these things. Who has understanding? Let him know them. For the ways of the Lord are right, and the righteous walk in them, but sinners fall in them.

notes.text: The KJV’s “calves of our lips” is praise offered like a sacrifice. The BSB reads ‘the fruit of our lips,’ as in Hebrews: “the sacrifice of praise to God continually, that is, the fruit of our lips” (Hebrews 13:15).

review.about: “Render the calves of our lips” is “offer our lips as calves for sacrifice”: the Hebrew has bulls (calves), and the note says what it means. “Take away all iniquity” has no “our” in the Hebrew, so none is added.
“Like the cedars of Lebanon” adds “the cedars of” (verses 5 and 6), as the BSB does, so he knows what Lebanon’s roots and fragrance are. Take it out if you’d rather not add.
The KJV adds “Ephraim shall say” (in italics: not in the Hebrew); the plain words keep it. The BSB has the Lord saying ‘O Ephraim, what have I to do anymore with idols?’ No note.
“The scent thereof” follows the KJV (“His fragrance”); the Hebrew word is usually ‘remembrance’ or ‘fame’ (BSB ‘His renown’). “Revive as the corn” is “come back to life like grain.”

verses: This is the word of the Lord that came to Joel, the son of Pethuel.
Hear this, you elders! Listen, everyone who lives in the land! Has anything like this happened in your days, or even in the days of your fathers?
Tell your children about it. Let your children tell their children, and their children tell the next generation.
What the devouring locust left, the swarming locust ate. What the swarming locust left, the young locust ate. And what the young locust left, the destroying locust ate.
Wake up and weep, you drunkards! Wail, all you who drink wine, because the new wine has been cut off from your mouths.
For a nation has come up against my land, strong and too many to count. Its teeth are a lion’s teeth, and it has the fangs of a lioness.
It has ruined my vine and splintered my fig tree. It has stripped off all its bark and thrown it away, and its branches are left white.
Mourn like a young bride dressed in sackcloth (rough cloth worn in mourning), grieving for her young husband.
The grain offering and the drink offering are cut off from the house of the Lord. The priests, who serve the Lord, are mourning.
The fields are ruined, and the land mourns, because the grain is ruined, the new wine is dried up, and the olive oil fails.
Be ashamed, you farmers! Wail, you who tend the vineyards, for the wheat and for the barley, because the harvest of the field is lost.
The vine is dried up, and the fig tree is withering. The pomegranate tree, the palm tree, and the apple tree—all the trees of the field are dried up. Truly, joy has dried up and left the people.

Put on sackcloth and mourn, you priests! Wail, you who serve at the altar! Come, spend the night in sackcloth, you who serve my God, because the grain offering and the drink offering are kept back from the house of your God.
Set apart a holy fast. Call a solemn assembly. Gather the elders and everyone who lives in the land into the house of the Lord your God, and cry out to the Lord.
How terrible that day will be! For the day of the Lord is near, and it will come like destruction from the Almighty.
Hasn’t the food been cut off right in front of our eyes—and joy and gladness from the house of our God?
The seeds have shriveled under the clods. The storehouses are ruined, and the barns are torn down, because the grain has dried up.
How the animals groan! The herds of cattle wander in confusion because they have no pasture. Even the flocks of sheep are suffering.
Lord, I cry out to you, because fire has burned up the pastures in the wilderness, and flames have burned all the trees of the field.
Even the wild animals cry out to you, because the streams of water have dried up, and fire has burned up the pastures in the wilderness.

notes.text: The KJV’s palmerworm, locust, cankerworm and caterpiller are four Hebrew words for locusts, perhaps kinds or stages of growth. The Church’s footnote says they picture invading armies. The BSB calls them devouring, swarming, young and destroying locusts.

review.about: The four locust names follow the BSB (devouring, swarming, young, destroying), with a note giving the KJV’s names. The same four are in Joel 2:25, in another order.

“A virgin … for the husband of her youth” is “a young bride … grieving for her young husband,” to keep it plain; the Hebrew pictures a young woman promised in marriage, mourning the man she was to marry. Sackcloth is explained, as in the Isaiah chapters.
“The cheek teeth of a great lion” is “the fangs of a lioness,” the Hebrew word’s meaning (BSB too).
“Meat offering” is “grain offering” (verses 9 and 13); in the KJV, meat means food. “Old men” (verse 2) is “elders,” as the Church’s footnote has it.

verses: Blow the trumpet in Zion! Sound the alarm on my holy mountain! Let everyone who lives in the land tremble, for the day of the Lord is coming; it is near—

a day of darkness and gloom, a day of clouds and thick darkness. Like the dawn spreading over the mountains comes a great and strong people. There has never been anything like it, and there will never be again, through the years of many generations.
In front of them a fire burns everything up, and behind them a flame blazes. The land in front of them is like the garden of Eden, but behind them it is a ruined wilderness. Nothing escapes them.
They look like horses, and they run like horsemen.
They leap over the mountaintops with a noise like chariots, like the crackle of fire burning up straw, like a strong army lined up for battle.
At the sight of them people will be in great pain; every face will turn dark.
They run like mighty men; they climb the wall like soldiers. Each one marches straight ahead, and they do not break their ranks.
They don’t push one another; each one walks in his own path. When they rush into the weapons, they are not wounded.
They rush through the city. They run along the wall. They climb up into the houses and go in through the windows like a thief.
The earth shakes in front of them, and the heavens tremble. The sun and the moon grow dark, and the stars stop shining.

The Lord raises His voice in front of His army, for His camp is very large, and the one who carries out His word is mighty. For the day of the Lord is great and very dreadful. Who can live through it?
Yet even now, says the Lord, turn to me with all your heart, with fasting, weeping, and mourning.
Tear your heart, and not your clothes, and turn to the Lord your God. For He is gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and full of kindness, and He turns away from sending disaster.
Who knows? He may turn and hold it back, and leave a blessing behind Him—a grain offering and a drink offering for the Lord your God.
Blow the trumpet in Zion. Set apart a holy fast. Call a solemn assembly.

Gather the people. Make the congregation holy. Bring together the elders, and gather the children, even the babies still nursing. Let the bridegroom come out of his room and the bride out of her chamber.

Let the priests, who serve the Lord, weep between the porch and the altar. Let them say, “Spare your people, Lord. Don’t let your inheritance be put to shame, with the nations ruling over them. Why should they say among the peoples, ‘Where is their God?’”
Then the Lord will be zealous for His land and have pity on His people.
Yes, the Lord will answer His people: Look, I will send you grain, new wine, and olive oil, and you will be satisfied with them. I will never again make you a disgrace among the nations.

I will drive the northern army far away from you and push him into a dry, deserted land, with his front toward the east sea (the Dead Sea) and his back toward the western sea (the Mediterranean). His stink will rise, and his foul smell will go up, because he has done great things.
Don’t be afraid, land! Be glad and rejoice, for the Lord will do great things.
Don’t be afraid, you wild animals, for the pastures in the wilderness are turning green. The trees are bearing their fruit, and the fig tree and the vine are giving their full harvest.

Be glad, then, you children of Zion, and rejoice in the Lord your God, for He has given you the early rain in the right amount. He will send down rain for you—the early rain and the latter rain—in the first month.
The threshing floors will be full of wheat, and the vats will overflow with new wine and olive oil.
I will restore to you the years eaten by the swarming locust, the young locust, the destroying locust, and the devouring locust, my great army that I sent among you.
You will eat plenty and be satisfied, and you will praise the name of the Lord your God, who has done wonders for you. And my people will never be put to shame.
Then you will know that I am among Israel, and that I am the Lord your God, and there is no other. And my people will never be put to shame.
And afterward I will pour out my Spirit on all people. Your sons and your daughters will prophesy, your old men will dream dreams, and your young men will see visions.
Even on the servants, men and women, I will pour out my Spirit in those days.
I will show wonders in the heavens and on the earth: blood, fire, and columns of smoke.
The sun will be turned into darkness and the moon into blood before the great and terrible day of the Lord comes.
And whoever calls on the name of the Lord will be delivered. For on mount Zion and in Jerusalem there will be deliverance, as the Lord has said, and among the remnant whom the Lord calls.

notes.text: Where the KJV says the Lord “repenteth him of the evil,” the Joseph Smith Translation says ‘he will turn away the evil from you.’ It also has the people repent, here and in verse 14.

The KJV says “the former rain moderately.” The Hebrew says the early rain is given ‘for righteousness,’ and the BSB reads ‘for your vindication.’ The Hebrew word for the early rain also means a teacher.
When the angel Moroni came to Joseph Smith in 1823, he quoted verses 28–32 and “said that this was not yet fulfilled, but was soon to be” (Joseph Smith—History 1:41).
On the day of Pentecost, when the disciples were filled with the Holy Ghost, Peter said, “this is that which was spoken by the prophet Joel” (Acts 2:16), and quoted verses 28–32 (Acts 2:17–21).
Paul quotes this verse to teach that the Lord is the same for Jew and Gentile: “whosoever shall call upon the name of the Lord shall be saved” (Romans 10:13).

review.about: “Repenteth him of the evil” is “turns away from sending disaster,” close to the Joseph Smith Translation (note) and to how the approved Jeremiah 18:8 says it. Verse 14’s “return and repent” is “turn and hold it back.” Check you’re happy with both.
“All faces shall gather blackness” is kept (“every face will turn dark”); the Hebrew word is unsure, and the BSB has the opposite picture, ‘every face turns pale.’ No note.
“When they fall upon the sword, they shall not be wounded” is kept; the Hebrew verb is unsure, and the BSB reads ‘They burst through the defenses, never breaking ranks.’ No note.

“Jealous” is “zealous,” as the Church’s footnote has it (‘HEB zealous’), since “jealous” may mislead a child. The KJV’s future tense is kept in verses 18–19; the BSB reads them as past (‘Then the LORD became jealous’).
The east sea and the “utmost” (western) sea are named in a few words. “Because he hath done great things” keeps the KJV’s “he,” the northern army; the BSB makes it ‘He,’ the Lord. Your call.

Two notes on verse 28 (Moroni and Peter), and Paul under verse 32. “All flesh” is “all people”; “handmaids” (verse 29) is “servants, men and women.” “My Spirit” is capitalized, as in the plain words for Isaiah 44:3.

verses: For look, in those days and at that time, when I bring back the captives of Judah and Jerusalem,

I will gather all nations and bring them down into the valley of Jehoshaphat (which means the Lord judges). There I will put them on trial for my people, my inheritance Israel, whom they scattered among the nations, and for dividing up my land.
They cast lots for my people. They traded a boy for a harlot and sold a girl for wine to drink.

Now what do you want with me, Tyre and Zidon and all the regions of Palestine (the land of the Philistines)? Are you paying me back for something? If you pay me back, I will quickly turn your payback on your own heads.
For you took my silver and my gold and carried my finest treasures into your temples.
You sold the people of Judah and Jerusalem to the Grecians (the Greeks), to send them far from their own land.
Look, I will stir them up to come out of the places where you sold them, and I will turn your payback on your own heads.
I will sell your sons and your daughters into the hands of the people of Judah, and they will sell them to the Sabeans, a nation far away. The Lord has spoken.
Announce this among the Gentiles: Get ready for war! Wake up the mighty men! Let all the soldiers come near and march up!
Beat your plowshares into swords and your pruning hooks into spears. Let the weak say, “I am strong.”
Hurry and come, all you nations around, and gather together. Lord, bring your mighty ones down there!
Let the nations wake up and come up to the valley of Jehoshaphat, for there I will sit to judge all the nations around.
Swing the sickle, for the harvest is ripe. Come, go down and tread the grapes, for the winepress is full and the vats overflow, because their wickedness is great.
Multitudes, multitudes in the valley of decision! For the day of the Lord is near in the valley of decision.
The sun and the moon will grow dark, and the stars will stop shining.
The Lord will roar from Zion and raise His voice from Jerusalem, and the heavens and the earth will shake. But the Lord will be a shelter for His people and a stronghold for the children of Israel.
Then you will know that I am the Lord your God, who lives in Zion, my holy mountain. Jerusalem will be holy, and strangers will never pass through her again.

On that day the mountains will drip with new wine, the hills will flow with milk, and all the streams of Judah will run with water. A spring will flow out from the house of the Lord and water the valley of Shittim (acacia trees).
Egypt will become a ruin, and Edom a desert wasteland, because of the violence done to the people of Judah, because they shed innocent blood in their land.
But people will live in Judah forever, and in Jerusalem from generation to generation.
For I will cleanse their blood that I have not cleansed, for the Lord lives in Zion.

notes.text: The KJV says “I will cleanse their blood.” The Hebrew word means to declare innocent or to leave unpunished, and the BSB reads ‘I will avenge their blood, which I have not yet avenged.’

review.about: “Given a boy for an harlot” keeps the KJV’s “harlot,” as you decided for Isaiah 1:21; it is the plainest modest word here. Check it suits Javan.
A few words are added for Jehoshaphat (‘the Lord judges’), Palestine (verse 4), the Grecians (verse 6) and Shittim (verse 18). “Plead with them” (argue a case, as in court) is “put them on trial.”
“The hope of his people, and the strength of the children of Israel” follows the Hebrew, “a shelter … and a stronghold” (BSB ‘a refuge … a stronghold’).
Hard Hebrew. The plain words keep the KJV’s “cleanse,” with a note for the BSB’s ‘avenge.’
This turns around Isaiah 2:4 and Micah 4:3 (“beat their swords into plowshares”); no note, since the README’s note kinds don’t include it.

treasure.means: To get engaged: to promise to marry someone. Here the Lord promises to make Israel His bride forever.
treasure.more: Even after Israel was unfaithful, the Lord promised a new engagement “in righteousness, and in judgment, and in lovingkindness, and in mercies.” His covenant love is that faithful.

treasure.means: To turn around and come back. It’s the Old Testament’s main word for repenting: turning away from sin and back to God.
treasure.more: Hosea says the Lord who has “torn” will also “heal us” and “bind us up.” Repenting means coming home to the Savior, who heals.

treasure.means: To ransom: to pay the price so that someone who is held captive can go free.
treasure.more: Paul echoes this verse when he teaches about the Resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:55). Jesus Christ paid the price to free us from death and the grave.

treasure.means: Something given freely, because you want to and not because you have to. It’s also the word for a freewill offering.
treasure.more: The Lord says, “I will love them freely.” His love isn’t a payment Israel earned. It’s a gift He chooses to give.

treasure.means: A trumpet made from a ram’s horn. It was blown to sound a warning or to call all the people together.
treasure.more: Joel’s shofar warns that “the day of the LORD cometh.” In verse 15 it sounds again, calling everyone to fast, gather, and turn back to God.

treasure.means: To pour out, like water poured from a jar. God promises to pour His Spirit on sons and daughters, young and old.
treasure.more: The angel Moroni quoted this prophecy to Joseph Smith and said it was soon to be fulfilled (Joseph Smith—History 1:41).
